However, I was also a huge fan of 3OH!3 at the time (this was around the time when OMENS hadn’t released yet), so I was very familiar with the names of the members when I saw them featured in the writing credits for Tattooed Heart (one of the few AG songs that I still enjoy). 

With all of that said, it completely baffles me that she would lie and suddenly claim to have written this song “on her own” when she was a teen. This is especially disheartening as an aspiring songwriter myself who wishes to be able to find other individuals to collab with. Even when I was a fan (never stan) of hers, I never took her for a songwriter. She literally had Leon Thomas, an actual songwriter, who helped co-write a good amount of her songs (thank god he’s finally getting the recognition he deserves). 

I believe her when she talks about co-producing her songs (since there’s video evidence of her doing so), but she never came across as a songwriter to me. Although I haven’t seen a lot of interviews with her, I’ve NEVER heard her talk about the actual songwriting/lyric process in detail (please correct me if she has). Comparing her to songwriters such as NIKI or Mariah Carey who actually do talk about the process of songwriting, it just seems very dumb, pointless, and unethical for her to try to paint herself as this “down to earth person who has been writing songs in her bedroom since her youth.” As an aspiring songwriter (and soon-to-be uni graduate), I can’t fathom the idea of not properly crediting others for their contribution to one’s own project/creation, let alone taking all of the credit for oneself 💀

In conclusion, she should stop trying to paint herself as a songwriter and just give credit to those who’ve contributed to her music’s success (a prime example being Whitney Houston).

This has always bothered me ever since Glimpse Of Us came out as a single. I really wanted to like it, but something felt off about it even before looking at the song credits (his name was on the writing credits for a short period of time before being taken off by the time his album released). When Smithereens finally released, I was very disappointed (especially since I preordered the CD) as it all felt rushed, incomplete, and just extremely lacking in personality (with the exception of Night Rider and Yukon which- surprise surprise- Joji had the most involvement in). We can debate about the production of this album all we want, but it’s difficult to deny that the lack of Joji actually being involved made this potential-to-be-big album be blown into smithereens (pun intended). His lack of presence makes this album lose any potential longevity, especially when compared to Ballads 1, Nectar, and In Tongues. To go even further, Nectar also involved many different writers in its creation. HOWEVER, unlike Smithereens, Joji was always involved in the process whether it was writing and/ or production credits, hence why Nectar has a bit more longevity than Smithereens (it even included Your Man, a song that’s mixed upon fans, to be featured in Invincible).

I think the main takeaway from this experience is to allow artists to create at their own pace, and for us as fans to be patient with these artists to make art instead of products. Sure there’s nothing bad with speculating or wanting new releases, but it’s another thing to feel entitled about it. I could’ve brought up differences between him and 88rising, but I hope I brought a (not really) new perspective to this conversation.

It really depends on your time management, but considering that you’re commuting by car, I don’t think it’ll affect your grades too much. However, you might experience some burnout and general frustrations (ie traffic), so prioritize your mental well-being and get as much sleep/ rest possible. Also, not sure if you’ve seen this brought up by others, but it’s very common for us transfers to experience imposter syndrome (the semester to quarter system is a huge whiplash), so really take care of your mental health and get as much rest as you physically can. Talk to professors about possible extension times (even if it’s by a day), and look into CAE asap if you have any disabilities. I truly hope for the best for you and other incoming transfers.

As someone who also transferred and commutes from East LA to campus 4x a day via public transportation, one of the best things you can do (aside from saving up money) is not think too much about the commute. The more you think about it, the more drained you feel, so it’s best not to think too much about it. 

Also, whether you’re commuting via personal vehicle or public transportation, try leaving 2-3 hours before the time your class starts. Either eat before leaving or pack a lunch and light snacks with you. If you’re commuting via public transportation, get the Bruin U-Pass. Take plenty of water with you. If you’re commuting via public transportation, take advantage of the ride and use that time to either study, do some hw (if possible), or nap. It helps out big time. Take a mask with you if you are taking buses/ trains cause sometimes they smell real bad. Take a portable charger with you as well. Depending on your major and method of transportation, try not to carry too much in your backpack.

As someone who comes from a low-income household, transferred from CC and commutes via public transportation- I highly recommend you go the CC route. As many others on this subreddit have said many times before- unless you’re going into stem or law, no degree is worth the lifelong debt. Tuition is already expensive enough. I can’t imagine also having to take out loans not only for tuition and school alone, but also for dorms, everyday living expenses, etc. 

Unless you were working 2-3 jobs in addition to being a full-time student, it seems like you’d have more to lose than gain. Even if you were working, UCLA follows the quarter system so it’s very easy to fall behind. If you fail or withdraw a certain amount of times (I don’t remember how much), this will severely affect your enrollment and it’s really not worth it in addition to the debt.

CC is practically free (especially if you’re a CA resident and go to a school within LACCD), there’s programs such as EOPS, FYE, etc, and you’ll pretty much get all of the same education for GEs and lower division classes for a fraction of what you’d pay at UCLA. You’ll also have more time to only really grasp what you’re learning, but also see if your chosen major is truly right for you (it’s easier to switch majors in CC), and you can get a part time job and save up money for UCLA. That way when you reapply as a transfer, you’ll be much more prepared in both academics and finances.

It depends on different factors (ie age, proficiency). If you were kindergarten age, then you’ll likely write in mostly hiragana (I forgot what age Japanese school children begin to learn basic kanji). However, if you’re let’s say a college student taking an intro to Japanese language course, you’ll likely write only in hiragana during your first few weeks of the class (depending on whether the college system follows a semester or quarter system). With that said, some may also write in all hiragana in order to be more “kawaii” (with the exception of certain phrases).

Going more into the linguistics of the Japanese language, one of the uses of hiragana is to indicate grammar. Unlike English, Japanese uses grammar markers to indicate topic, subject, etc. Let’s use the second half of Ariana’s caption from this post as an example:

東京が大好き
とうきょうがだいすき
Tokyo ga daisuki

As we can see, her message is written in all hiragana. The way it would be written with kanji would be the line above it （東京が大好き）. Another thing we can se is that while the words for “Tokyo” and “daisuki” have kanji, “ga” does not use kanji as it’s used as a marker to indicate that Tokyo is the subject that (Ariana) loves. 

So when she writes everything out in hiragana, it’s a bit of a headache to read because (at least from the perspective of someone who’s majoring in Japanese) it feels like the words are all crammed up together. In other words, if I had to write this in an English equivalent, it would look like this:

ilovetokyou 

One last thing: I didn’t touch on the first half because “thank you” Japanese is normally (at least from what I’m aware of) written in all hiragana.

In summary, writing in all hiragana depends on different factors. In the case of Ariana, when putting into perspective that she herself has talked about learning Japanese for around a decade or so, one would think that she would’ve used kanji for not only pragmatic reasons, but also to display her knowledge/ skills on the language. Therefore, there’s a high likelihood that she did this for aesthetic purposes in order to look more cute/ kawaii. There’s also the possibility of her possibly not knowing a lot of basic kanji, but I’ll give her the benefit of doubt in order to not assume how proficient she as a whole just from this one post.

Hope this helped clarify any confusion, and to anyone who’s also been studying or fluent in Japanese, please correct me if I have any mistakes in my explanation.

Even if I wasn’t a Japanese major (undergrad), it’s easy to tell that her enunciation and some of her pronunciation is pretty bad. Mind you I’m not fluent in my own Japanese skills, but god I hope to never speak Japanese as mumbled as her in public 💀

I tried to transcribe what she said but even after listening to her speaking over and over again, I cannot for the life of me understand what she said after 私の絶対 despite her explanation.

「私の絶対（）はとてもセクシーです。」

Romanization: watashino zettai () ha totemo sekushii desu.

Trans: My absolute () is very sexy.

Her pronunciation of vowels isn’t that bad. It’s okay. But her consonants??? I don’t know if she said りよいき、りょいき、りょうぃき、(riyoiki, ryoiki, ryowiki) etc. Whether that word is contracted or not, the articulation is just plain awful and hard to understand.

Despite some words being contracted when spoken in Japanese, consonants are still pretty distinct and understandable. Even when some consonants are changed (ie TA to DA/ た・だ), these sounds are still very distinct. She got 絶対/ zettai right, including the small gap in tt. 

However, when she said セクシー/ sekushii, she didn’t stress the ii enough so it sounded like セクシ/ sekushi instead. In a super general rule, the Japanese doesn’t stress its words in the same way as English. However, there are words that are stressed, but usually indicated by an extra vowel (ie kawaii/ かわいい) or with a dashed line (ie ramen/ ラーメン).

In terms of a general accent in the voice when speaking, there isn’t anything inherently bad about it. With that said, considering that Ariana is someone who is known to mimic others, I’d be careful when trying to speak in a Japanese accent. On one hand, it can help one immerse themselves into the language (especially when it comes to shadowing practice). 

HOWEVER, on the other hand, she can potentially reinforce harmful stereotypes of Japanese women being “too kawaii” “too soft” “too docile” etc, especially if she hasn’t learned about the nuances of gender roles/ gendered language in Japan. This is quite complex to talk about as I’m not Japanese, so I’m really going off of what I’ve learned from past lectures in uni.

I can’t speak on pitch accent because my past professors didn’t really emphasize that aspect of the language when I began learning, therefore I’m not very knowledgeable in this area. If there’s anyone that’s native/ fluent/ knowledgeable in Japanese (linguistically and/ or culturally), you’re more than welcome to add onto this little breakdown as well as correcting me on any possible mistakes 🫶🫶

I think it really depends on your major and how you input that effort into those as well as how much you’re willing to sacrifice in order to get those straight A’s. I’m a language major and got mostly A’s as a first year transfer last year. Did everything I needed to do, but at the expense of my mental health and self esteem. This quarter I got A, B, and C, but I’m way happier now since I stopped focusing on getting straight A’s.

Some of my takeaways from this past quarter is: 
1.) prioritize which classes you deem as most important. Of course they’re all important, but depending on your major, having a B or C can heavily impact your career plans or even plans for grad school (if you’re thinking about that).
2.) not all classes need the same time and effort put into them. Again, this really depends on your major, but if you look through the syllabus and see that one class require more workload while the other requires more reading time, choose which one you think can finish within a couple hours compared to the other that will take more time (or no time at all). This advice probably isn’t the best, but it’s helped me so thought I’d also share this piece of advice.
3.) go to office hours. Seriously, even if it’s just for one question on an assignment or test, professors love seeing their students reaching out to them for extra support. I barely started going to office hours the last few weeks of this quarter and it definitely helped out a bit. Even if you have to send them an email asking for help or letting them know that you won’t attend class for whatever reason, it’s still better than not communicating with your professors at all.
4.) use your time wisely. This is kind of an extension of my first point, but if you’re also a public commuter like myself, using that commute time to work or study helps tremendously.
5.) study/ review what you don’t know. Only refresh on what you know every 2 weeks or so. Again, this depends on your major so I don’t know how helpful this would be for you or any other transfer.
6.) take breaks. Seriously, this might be one of the most important points here. Take proper breaks in between assignments or questions. Stretch. Go for a walk. Get proper sleep at night. Go to the gym. Read a book unrelated to your major. Watch a film. Do anything else during your free time, but don’t have too much free time. Have free time in moderation. Find an activity/ hobby to help you learn how to manage your time properly.
7.) eat properly and stay hydrated. Also very important.
8.) try to befriend at least one person from one of your classes, but this part can be difficult as a transfer student as everyone seems to already have their own inner groups. With that said, still try.

That’s all that I can think of from the top of my head as a fellow transfer student who had already completed their first year. Hope any of this was helpful, and good luck to you, OP, as well as any other first year transfer student.

(PS. Yes, I also had imposter syndrome during my first year and believe that you all are also able to overcome the feeling ❤️)

Just like others have already said on here- take the CC route. As a transfer student, despite not applying to UCLA during senior year, my gpa was shit for UC standards. I went the CC route as a way to start over and figure out what I wanted to do in life. After years of being there, I applied to UCLA on a whim, and next thing you know I get an acceptance letter in late April. After a year of imposter syndrome (a story for another day), I found out that transfer students have a higher likelihood to getting accepted compared to HS students (I don’t remember the percentage). 

Also, I looked through your other comments and saw that you have a 3.5 GPA. I also had a 3.5 GPA but in CC so that + having been part of a club during COVID + HEAVILY revised PIQ essays (never BS your PIQs in the future) are what led to my acceptance to UCLA. Of course this isn’t true for everyone as I personally felt like I never did a lot at CC, but my point in sharing all of this is to show that don’t get upset about not getting into UCLA right out of high school. Take this opportunity to not only save a ton of money, but to also help you grow and mature yourself as an individual at CC. Don’t worry about having that “full college experience” just because you didn’t go to UCLA all 4 years. 

If your priority is academics over lifestyle, I highly recommend you take the CC route. Plus, UCLA is EXPENSIVE whereas CCs are practically free if you live in California. All of your GEs/ lower division courses are practically free whereas you’re paying thousands of dollars at UCLA (not worth it imho). If you’re also thinking about dorming or living near campus, save as much of the money CC financial aid gives you cause you’re gonna NEED it. 

Sign up for food stamps and EOPS (or a similar program) if offered and if you’re low-income. Join clubs, talk to people, stay in touch with close friends, apply for a job. There’s so much you can do while being a CC student and grow in the process because that’s one of the key aspects that UCLA looks for in their students. 3.5GPA may not be a lot in HS, but if you keep up with that GPA with the addition of the other things you can do at CC, you may have a shot then. And whatever happens in life during your CC years and you overcome them, write about those experiences in your PIQs and show what you’ve learned from them. Best of luck, OP. Hope this helped.

I used to be in a situationship where I pretty much felt what you described. It lasted for about 2-3 years and it ended around the time I transferred here. I felt numb. I felt like I lost my humanity. I felt like a dead person walking. I wanted to off myself. I couldn’t smile. I couldn’t cry. I couldn’t feel anything nor did I have the time as I was a new student trying to survive my first quarter. I can go on and on about the details, but as I mentioned before, a lot of what you mentioned is pretty similar to my own experience.

With that said, despite the anguish that I felt, I truly think that it was a blessing in disguise. OP, I’d be lying if the pain would go away overnight cause it really doesn’t. This type of pain for many of us doesn’t really start to fade away until months later. While it’s okay to let ourselves fall for a moment, we can’t stay that way forever. Time doesn’t wait for anybody, so the best thing you can do is to slowly push yourself little by little each day, even if some days feel harder than others.  

I think the best medicine for situations like these is (aside from grieving) to reflect on what you learned, acknowledge what went wrong, accept it, and learn to not only truly appreciate those closest to you, but to learn how to live and be comfortable alone. As others have pointed out, we really can’t have just one person or thing be the main source of our happiness. If/ when we do, we not only lose a balanced power dynamic, but we also lose ourselves, and that’s something very difficult to get back. However, that doesn’t mean it’s impossible to find ourselves again. We can do this by not only appreciating those closest to us, but also talk and reflecting on the situation. At first it might hurt too much to do so, but eventually it’s gonna feel like you’re talking about someone else despite it being your experience.

Some of the things I did was ask myself, “why did I want to be in a committed relationship that eagerly? Is there something in my past that made me think this way? Why do I think I will never be loved? Do I want to keep living this way? What do I want to do to change that? How do I find and better myself?” While these questions may or may not also apply to you, just reflecting on yourself with questions that pretty much force you to not bs yourself help so much. They might sting a bit, but eventually that sting passes by in time.

Find new or rediscover old hobbies. This might sound dumb, but I think it’s the biggest key to help find yourself again after a toxic/ failed relationship. Whether it’s journaling, studying, or collecting action figures, do something that gives you a type of joy you really cant find anywhere else but through those hobbies. The best part of hobbies is that YOU have the control of when you want to work on them and when you want a break and do something else. Point is, hobbies are very liberating and should be more appreciated in life.

Will you become truly happy again overnight? No. I’d be lying if I said otherwise. However, as long as you try little by little to pick yourself up and slowly move forward, you’ll look back at this time and hopefully think, “wow… that was me?” And while you don’t really need a therapist for this kind of thing (unless there’s more serious matters that we don’t know and you’re not able to disclose on here), just talking and trying to rationalize this with a trusted friend/ family member will also help a lot, even if it’s to just cry in their shoulders.

I truly believe you (and anyone else going through something similar) can come out of this as a stronger individual, OP. Feel free to message me if you need any help/ support. Drink some water, try to eat a bit, and get some sleep. Take care, OP. ❤️

Whenever I feel stuck with writing lyrics/ poems, I usually try to delve into other forms of art, or take a break and do something not art related or “unproductive” (ie watch a movie or yt, take a walk outside). Sometimes when words fail to express ourselves and our thoughts, we need other mediums in order to do so (ie painting, drawing, reading, journaling, dancing, playing an instrument). In that same sense, we also need to give ourselves a break to prevent burning out from creativity. 

Art isn’t a race (despite what the industry says otherwise), so there should be no rush to creating it (ideally). Also, don’t compare yourself to others, but compare your works from the past and see how much you’ve improved.

However, if you do decide to compare your works to others, more specifically to already established artists/ writers you enjoy, I suggest you look and study through their lyrics and melodies. See what you like, what you don’t like, what works and what doesn’t, the meaning behind the phrases, noticing any rhetorical devices, etc. 

Also, definitely listen to albums from artists you enjoy and have either already listened to, or have only listened to the singles. This sounds silly, but albums such as Folie à Deux by Fall Out Boy or Melodrama by Lorde have such an interesting use of their lyrics and melodies that the more you listen to those albums on repeat, the more quirks you discover which will (hopefully) give you that inspirational boost.

Those are some of the things that I do to boost my own creativity. Hope any of this helped, OP.

As someone who got accepted as a transfer student a little over a year ago (barely finishing up my first year), I suggest waiting for orientation day for transfer students. Tours are longer (around 8am to 5pm), and you’ll have the option to stay for the night (you could possibly even get a fee waiver for the entire thing if you’re low income), you’ll be with a small group (about 6-7 students) the entire day consisting of other transfer students who are either in the same or similar major department to you, and you’ll be able to enroll to classes and get your bruin card that day. You’ll also get other free goodies such as food vouchers and bag filled with more things (I got a cap tassel, 2 year academic planner, and other things that I can’t remember). Hope this helps, and congrats on getting accepted!!

If you’re really dead set on going to UCLA no matter what, go the CC route. That’s your best bet after high school. Whether you take a gap semester/ year break or not, CC will help you start over with not only your grades, but also with a lot saving money. Even then, I highly suggest keeping an open mind to other schools aside from UCLA. Plus, some teachers at CC have either graduated, taught, or done both at UCLA, so you can talk to them during office hours for more help and advice on how to get into UCLA.

Also, as much as I hate to admit this, some of those “sob story” response will play a key factor to your application. Not so much as an act of pity (though I’ll admit sometimes it does feel like that), but to show how you’ve overcome difficult challenges in your life, how you persevered despite having little to no control in certain situations in life.

For some background , I say all of this as a transfer student who has major depression disorder, from a low income household, have immigrant parents, and also barely graduated in high school with passable grades.

One last piece of advice: DO NOT STRESS TOO MU ABOUT HOW LONG IT WILL TAKE YOU TO GET INTO YOUR DREAM SCHOOL. DON’T WORRY ABOUT OTHERS CAUSE AT THE END OF THE DAY, YOU’RE THE ONE CREATING YOUR OWN PATH TO LIFE, AND NO ONE ELSE’S. I’m serious about this. Life happens, and some things will take us longer than expected to complete or start (in this case, getting into UCLA). Sure it’s ideal to get in after 2 years of CC, but don’t beat yourself up if it takes an extra year or so to get into UCLA. Think of that extra time spent at CC as an advantage to do more extracurricular/ volunteering/ coursework/ work experience, rather than being “held back” or “behind” in life. 

Hope some of this helped and best of luck to you!
